title: Living With Diabetes: GP Care & Monitoring
h1: Living With Diabetes: GP Monitoring & Long-Term Management
description: Understand diabetes check-ups, HbA1c, kidneys, feet and eye care, and how GP follow-up supports long-term health in Woolloongabba.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles living with diabetes gp monitoring long term management
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Chronic Disease Management Living With Diabetes: GP Monitoring & Long-Term Management Understand diabetes check-ups, HbA1c, kidneys, feet and eye care, and how GP follow-up supports long-term health in Woolloongabba. Introduction Living with diabetes involves more than checking a single blood glucose reading. A practical long-term care plan considers glucose trends, heart and kidney health, medicines, daily routines and the complications that can develop gradually. Your GP can work with you to agree on goals that fit your health and circumstances. Why This Topic Matters Diabetes affects blood vessels and nerves over time. Regular review can identify changes early and create opportunities to adjust treatment, address cardiovascular risks and organise appropriate screening. HbA1c reflects average glucose over roughly two to three months, but the right target differs between patients. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: Blood glucose readings repeatedly outside the personalised range agreed with your clinician. Changes in vision, tingling or loss of sensation in the feet, or wounds that heal slowly. Thirst, frequent urination, recurrent infections or unexpected weight change. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Arrange a GP appointment for new symptoms, repeated low or high glucose readings, medicine side effects or missed diabetes reviews. A foot wound, especially with redness or infection, needs prompt assessment. Severe confusion, collapse, vomiting with dehydration or symptoms of a serious glucose emergency require urgent care or 000. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review HbA1c, blood pressure, kidney tests, lipid management, medicine use and individual nutrition or movement goals. Care may also involve retinal examinations, foot assessments, diabetes education and referrals to allied health. Where appropriate, a GP chronic condition management plan can coordinate follow-up under current Medicare rules. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions How often should HbA1c be checked? The interval depends on diabetes type, treatment changes, stability and individual targets. Your GP will advise a suitable schedule rather than using one interval for everyone. Is a foot check important if my feet feel normal? Yes. Some nerve and circulation changes have few early symptoms. Your care team can recommend examination and self-care based on your risk. Can diabetes management include other professionals? Yes. Depending on need, a diabetes educator, dietitian, podiatrist, optometrist or specialist may contribute to coordinated care. title: GP Chronic Care Plans Explained
h1: Understanding GP Chronic Disease Care Plans
description: Learn how GP chronic condition management plans work in Australia, when they may help and what coordinated long-term care involves.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles understanding gp chronic disease care plans
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Chronic Disease Management Understanding GP Chronic Disease Care Plans Learn how GP chronic condition management plans work in Australia, when they may help and what coordinated long-term care involves. Introduction People living with conditions such as diabetes, asthma, chronic heart disease or arthritis may need more than one-off appointments. A GP chronic condition management plan brings health priorities, treatment steps, review dates and coordinated services together with the patient's agreement. Why This Topic Matters Australia introduced a revised GP chronic condition management plan framework from 1 July 2025, replacing the earlier GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement structure for new plans. The framework supports planned care but does not guarantee that every person or allied health visit will be Medicare-funded. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: One or more diagnosed long-term conditions require regular treatment or monitoring. Several clinicians are involved and information or appointments are becoming difficult to coordinate. Your goals, medicines or functional needs have changed since the previous care plan. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Discuss a plan if ongoing conditions affect your life or you need clearer coordination. You can also ask for a review if an existing plan is out of date. New severe symptoms should be medically assessed promptly rather than waiting for a planning appointment. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can assess whether a structured plan is appropriate, document health conditions and agreed goals, review medicines and monitoring, and identify relevant services. Review appointments help check whether the plan still fits. Medicare item eligibility, referrals and any out-of-pocket costs should be confirmed for your circumstances. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Are these the same as the old GP Management Plans? No. New GP chronic condition management plans replaced the previous GPMP/TCA items from July 2025, with transitional arrangements for some existing plans. Does a plan mean all allied health is free? No. Medicare eligibility and the number of subsidised services are regulated, and allied health providers may charge gaps. Can a plan be updated? Yes. A plan is intended to be reviewed as needs, medicines or treatment goals change. title: Blood Pressure Explained: GP Checks
description: What do blood pressure numbers mean? Learn about high blood pressure, home readings and when to seek GP advice in Brisbane.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Chronic Disease Management Blood Pressure Explained What do blood pressure numbers mean? Learn about high blood pressure, home readings and when to seek GP advice in Brisbane. Introduction Blood pressure measures the force of blood against artery walls. Your reading has two numbers: systolic pressure when the heart contracts and diastolic pressure when it relaxes. One elevated reading does not always establish a diagnosis, because stress, activity and measurement technique can influence the result. Why This Topic Matters Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney problems even when you feel well. Lower blood pressure can also matter when associated with dizziness or falls. Diagnosis and treatment use repeated, correctly measured readings and individual risk factors. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: Repeated higher-than-expected readings at home, pharmacy or the clinic. Dizziness or feeling faint when standing, particularly after medicine changes. Family history of early cardiovascular disease, diabetes or kidney disease that raises the importance of risk assessment. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP appointment to review repeated elevated readings, possible medicine side effects or uncertainty about home measurements. Severe headache with neurological symptoms, chest pain, major breathlessness or suspected stroke needs emergency assistance: call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP may repeat measurements, suggest home or ambulatory monitoring, review medicines and check heart, kidney or diabetes risk as appropriate. Treatment can include activity, salt reduction, limiting alcohol, medicines and follow-up. Your target and review timing depend on your broader health. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Can high blood pressure cause no symptoms? Yes. Many people with hypertension feel entirely well. That is why opportunistic checks can be useful. Is a single high reading a diagnosis? Usually not. Your GP may consider repeated measurements and home or ambulatory readings. Should I stop my blood pressure tablets if a reading is normal? Do not change prescribed medicines without discussing the results and any symptoms with your treating clinician. title: Managing Asthma: GP Reviews & Action Plans
description: Understand asthma symptoms, preventer and reliever medicines, action plans and when to arrange a GP asthma review.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Chronic Disease Management Managing Asthma Understand asthma symptoms, preventer and reliever medicines, action plans and when to arrange a GP asthma review. Introduction Asthma causes inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Symptoms can change with respiratory infections, exercise, allergens or weather. Good management focuses on reducing symptoms, preventing attacks and making sure you know what to do when breathing changes. Why This Topic Matters People sometimes accept regular wheeze or night waking as normal, yet these can indicate poorly controlled asthma. An up-to-date written asthma action plan and correct inhaler technique can help make daily management safer. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: Wheeze, chest tightness, coughing or breathlessness that recurs or wakes you at night. Needing your reliever more often than the plan recommends. Difficulty exercising, or symptoms after smoke, pollen or respiratory infections. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Arrange review if symptoms are recurring, activity is limited or your inhaler use has increased. Follow your written asthma action plan during worsening symptoms. If breathing becomes severe, you struggle to speak, or symptoms do not improve with emergency action-plan steps, call 000. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review symptoms and triggers, check inhaler technique and adherence, arrange spirometry where suitable, and adjust evidence-based treatment. A written action plan explains routine care and what to do when symptoms worsen. Follow-up after an attack is particularly important. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need an asthma action plan? A written plan is recommended so you know which medicines to use and when to escalate care. Can asthma be present without obvious wheeze? Yes. Recurrent cough or breathlessness can occur, but other conditions can cause similar symptoms and require assessment. Should I change my inhaler dose myself? Only according to your personalised action plan or advice from your treating clinician. title: Understanding Cholesterol & Heart Risk
description: Learn what cholesterol results mean, how LDL and HDL relate to heart risk and how your GP may recommend prevention or treatment.
headings: Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients
When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Chronic Disease Management Understanding Cholesterol Learn what cholesterol results mean, how LDL and HDL relate to heart risk and how your GP may recommend prevention or treatment. Introduction Cholesterol is a fat-like substance used by the body. Blood tests usually report different types of cholesterol and triglycerides. A result makes more sense when considered alongside blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, family history and previous cardiovascular disease. Why This Topic Matters High LDL cholesterol can contribute to fatty deposits in blood vessels. Most people do not feel cholesterol rising. The reason for treatment is to reduce future cardiovascular risk, not simply to reach a number without context. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A blood test reports raised LDL cholesterol or triglycerides. A close relative experienced heart disease at a young age or has a hereditary lipid disorder. You have diabetes, kidney disease, high blood pressure or other cardiovascular risks. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a GP review after an abnormal result, particularly when there is strong family history or multiple risks. Sudden chest pressure, arm or jaw pain, fainting or suspected stroke symptoms are emergencies and require 000, regardless of previous cholesterol results. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can interpret lipid results, estimate overall risk where applicable, discuss diet, exercise and smoking cessation, and explain when cholesterol-lowering medicines may help. Additional tests or specialist review may be appropriate for very high levels or suspected inherited conditions. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Can I feel high cholesterol? Usually not. High cholesterol is generally detected through a blood test. Does a high total cholesterol result always mean I need tablets? Not necessarily. Decisions take your full risk profile and preferences into account. How soon should cholesterol be rechecked? The schedule depends on your results, treatment and cardiovascular risk; your GP can set the interval. title: Understanding Type 2 Diabetes
description: A diagnosis of type 2 diabetes can raise many questions.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Diabetes & Ongoing Care Understanding Type 2 Diabetes A diagnosis of type 2 diabetes can raise many questions. Understanding what the diagnosis means and how it is monitored can help you participate in decisions about your care. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction A diagnosis of type 2 diabetes can raise many questions. Understanding what the diagnosis means and how it is monitored can help you participate in decisions about your care. What Is It? Type 2 diabetes develops when the body has difficulty using insulin effectively and blood glucose becomes too high. Risk is influenced by family history, age, health conditions, sleep, activity and other factors. It is not a personal failure or simply the result of one food choice. Thirst or frequent urination High glucose found on a blood test Family history or other diabetes risk factors Should I Be Concerned? Some people notice thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, blurry vision or slow-healing wounds. Others have no obvious symptoms and are diagnosed through a blood test. Ask for assessment if you have symptoms or relevant risk factors. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Get urgent medical help for severe dehydration, vomiting with marked weakness, confusion, drowsiness or rapid breathing. If someone is collapsing or difficult to wake, call 000. People taking glucose-lowering medicines also need advice on low blood glucose management. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can explain blood tests including HbA1c, assess cardiovascular and kidney risks, discuss food, activity and medicine options, and arrange a review plan. Diabetes care is individual; goals and treatments change over time. Bring recent glucose results if available, medicine details and questions about long-term monitoring or referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can type 2 diabetes be present without symptoms? Yes. High blood glucose can be present before obvious symptoms develop. Screening is based on risk and individual circumstances. Will everyone need insulin? No. Treatment may involve lifestyle changes and tablets or other medicines; some people later need insulin. Decisions are individual. title: Living With Diabetes
description: Living with diabetes involves ordinary routines as well as medical appointments.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Diabetes & Ongoing Care Living With Diabetes Living with diabetes involves ordinary routines as well as medical appointments. A workable plan should fit your health needs, lifestyle and priorities rather than expecting perfect readings every day. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Living with diabetes involves ordinary routines as well as medical appointments. A workable plan should fit your health needs, lifestyle and priorities rather than expecting perfect readings every day. What Is It? Daily diabetes care may include food choices, movement, medicines, glucose monitoring and looking after feet. Sleep, work shifts, illness, travel and emotional wellbeing can affect management. People who take insulin or certain tablets may also need a plan to recognise and manage low blood glucose. Changes in home glucose readings Difficulty managing diabetes during work or travel Foot concerns or repeated low glucose Should I Be Concerned? If your readings change, you feel unwell, have repeated low-glucose episodes or are struggling with medicines or daily routines, arrange a review. Foot wounds, new tingling, blurred vision or persistent infections also need attention. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Get urgent medical help for severe low blood glucose causing confusion, seizure or unconsciousness, or serious symptoms of high blood glucose such as vomiting, rapid breathing and dehydration. Call 000 if there is collapse or impaired consciousness. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review treatment goals and how you are managing, organise appropriate tests and referrals, and help plan sick-day management. Support can include diabetes education, dietetics, podiatry and eye checks, depending on individual needs. Bring recent glucose results if available, medicine details and questions about long-term monitoring or referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need to check glucose every day? Monitoring needs vary by diabetes treatment and individual risk. Your GP or diabetes educator can explain whether finger-prick or sensor readings would help. Can I still enjoy meals with family? Usually yes. The focus is sustainable food patterns and individual treatment goals, not rigid rules or eliminating entire food groups without advice. title: Diabetes Monitoring Explained
description: Diabetes monitoring is about protecting health over time, not simply recording one glucose number.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Diabetes & Ongoing Care Diabetes Monitoring Explained Diabetes monitoring is about protecting health over time, not simply recording one glucose number. Different tests look at different aspects of diabetes care. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Diabetes monitoring is about protecting health over time, not simply recording one glucose number. Different tests look at different aspects of diabetes care. What Is It? HbA1c estimates average blood glucose over recent months. Blood pressure, cholesterol and kidney tests help assess cardiovascular and renal risk. Foot examinations look for circulation and nerve changes; regular eye assessments screen for diabetes-related eye disease. HbA1c and kidney test reviews Foot sensation or circulation concerns Eye checks or changing vision Should I Be Concerned? Review is important if you have not had checks for some time, have a new medicine, notice tingling or wounds in your feet, experience visual change or have difficulty understanding test results. Timing of tests is based on your health situation. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Sudden vision loss, confusion, severe dehydration, persistent vomiting or severe hypoglycaemia are urgent warning signs. Call 000 for a seizure, collapse or other life-threatening symptoms. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can develop a personalised schedule of HbA1c, blood pressure, kidney, foot and eye reviews, interpret changes together and coordinate with eye-care professionals, podiatrists and educators when appropriate. Bring recent glucose results if available, medicine details and questions about long-term monitoring or referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is HbA1c the same as a home glucose reading? No. HbA1c reflects a longer-term pattern; a home reading shows glucose at a particular time. Both have different uses. How often should my feet be checked? The frequency depends on your risks and findings. A GP or podiatrist can advise the appropriate schedule. title: Preventing Diabetes Complications
description: The purpose of long-term diabetes care is to reduce avoidable complications while supporting quality of life.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Diabetes & Ongoing Care Preventing Diabetes Complications The purpose of long-term diabetes care is to reduce avoidable complications while supporting quality of life. Small, realistic changes and regular review can make a meaningful difference. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction The purpose of long-term diabetes care is to reduce avoidable complications while supporting quality of life. Small, realistic changes and regular review can make a meaningful difference. What Is It? Diabetes can affect the eyes, kidneys, nerves, feet and cardiovascular system. Risk is influenced by glucose exposure over time, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking and other factors. Not everyone develops complications, and many risks can be reduced. Unhealed foot wounds Changes in eyesight or sensation High blood pressure or cholesterol alongside diabetes Should I Be Concerned? Book review for persistent high readings, changes in sight, numbness, foot skin breaks, new swelling or difficulty managing medicines. Prompt care for a foot wound can be particularly important in diabetes. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Seek same-day urgent care for a foot infection that spreads or causes fever, sudden vision change or severe illness. Call 000 for chest pain suggesting a heart attack, stroke symptoms, unconsciousness or severe metabolic symptoms. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review overall cardiovascular risk, tailor glucose and blood-pressure treatment, support smoking cessation where relevant, and schedule eye, kidney and foot screening. Referrals and follow-up should be based on identified risk rather than a fixed checklist for everyone. Bring recent glucose results if available, medicine details and questions about long-term monitoring or referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Are complications inevitable? No. Many people live well with diabetes, especially when risk factors are monitored and managed consistently. Can regular foot care help? Yes. Checking skin, footwear and sensation and treating injuries early can help reduce complications. Ask for advice tailored to your risk. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Diabetes & Ongoing Care Diabetes Care Plans Explained For some people, coordinating diabetes care is as important as choosing medicines. A GP chronic condition management plan may help document goals and clarify the roles of the care team. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction For some people, coordinating diabetes care is as important as choosing medicines. A GP chronic condition management plan may help document goals and clarify the roles of the care team. What Is It? In Australia, GP chronic condition management plans replaced older GP management plans and team care arrangements from 1 July 2025, with transition provisions for existing arrangements. Eligibility and Medicare-funded allied health access depend on current rules and individual circumstances. Coordinating several clinicians Questions about Medicare allied health referrals Long-term diabetes goals and reviews Should I Be Concerned? A care plan may be worth discussing if diabetes requires ongoing treatment, multiple clinicians are involved or you need help keeping track of referrals and review appointments. Having diabetes does not automatically guarantee a particular Medicare-funded service. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? A care plan is not a substitute for urgent medical assessment. Severe hypoglycaemia, chest pain, stroke signs or serious infection need emergency or urgent care rather than a routine plan review. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess eligibility, agree on care goals, document medicines and monitoring, coordinate appropriate allied health referrals and review progress. Reception can help with appointment length and general billing questions; clinical eligibility is assessed by the GP. Bring recent glucose results if available, medicine details and questions about long-term monitoring or referrals. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is a GP care plan automatically free? Not necessarily. Medicare eligibility, item requirements and the practice’s fee arrangements must be confirmed before the service. Do I need a new care plan every visit? No. Plans are reviewed and updated based on need and Medicare rules, not recreated at every ordinary appointment. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Blood Pressure & Heart Health High Blood Pressure Explained High blood pressure often causes no symptoms. Understanding what the readings mean is more useful than waiting to feel unwell. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction High blood pressure often causes no symptoms. Understanding what the readings mean is more useful than waiting to feel unwell. What Is It? Blood pressure has two numbers: systolic pressure while the heart beats and diastolic pressure while it relaxes. Diagnosis usually relies on repeated accurate measurements, sometimes including home or 24-hour monitoring, rather than one reading during a stressful day. Repeated elevated readings High blood pressure with other health conditions Questions about medication side effects Should I Be Concerned? See a GP if readings remain high, you have diabetes or kidney disease, or you have been advised to monitor pressure. Bring any home readings and details of medicines, including over-the-counter treatments. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call 000 if high blood pressure occurs with chest pain, severe breathlessness, confusion, new weakness, speech difficulty or sudden major visual change. Very high readings with severe symptoms need emergency assessment. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can check measurement technique, review cardiovascular risk and discuss medicines and practical approaches such as movement, lower-salt eating and limiting alcohol. Treatment targets depend on your overall health. Bring home blood-pressure readings, recent test results and an up-to-date list of prescribed and over-the-counter medicines. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Can I feel high blood pressure? Often not. Regular checks are important because high blood pressure may have no warning symptoms. Is a single high reading a diagnosis? Usually not. Clinicians consider repeated measurements and the setting in which they were taken. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources offer further general information. title: When Should I Be Concerned About Blood Pressure?
h1: When Should I Be Concerned About Blood Pressure?
description: One unusual blood-pressure reading can be unsettling.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles when should i be concerned about blood pressure
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Blood Pressure & Heart Health When Should I Be Concerned About Blood Pressure? One unusual blood-pressure reading can be unsettling. The important questions are whether it was measured correctly, whether it remains unusual and whether symptoms are present. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction One unusual blood-pressure reading can be unsettling. The important questions are whether it was measured correctly, whether it remains unusual and whether symptoms are present. What Is It? Blood pressure varies during the day, with activity, pain, stress and medicines. Readings can be affected by cuff size, arm position or measuring immediately after exercise. Persistently elevated readings deserve review even when you feel fine. Unexpected home readings Dizziness or fainting with medicines Readings outside the range advised by your GP Should I Be Concerned? Book a GP appointment if home readings remain above your advised range, treatment seems less effective, or you experience dizziness or fainting. Do not change prescribed blood-pressure medicines based on one reading without advice. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? If an abnormal reading is accompanied by chest pain, stroke-like symptoms, new confusion, significant shortness of breath or sudden vision changes, call 000. Symptoms take priority over repeating measurements at home. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can check the equipment, assess the series of readings and discuss whether 24-hour monitoring, medicine review or other tests are useful. A personal plan is especially important during pregnancy or with kidney disease. Bring home blood-pressure readings, recent test results and an up-to-date list of prescribed and over-the-counter medicines. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions When should I repeat a home reading? Sit quietly, use an appropriate cuff and follow the technique your healthcare professional recommends. Record several readings rather than relying on one. Can blood pressure be too low? Yes. Low blood pressure may cause dizziness or fainting. Sudden severe symptoms or collapse need urgent assessment. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Blood Pressure & Heart Health Heart Health Checks Heart health involves more than an ECG or cholesterol number. A preventive GP assessment considers multiple risk factors together. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Heart health involves more than an ECG or cholesterol number. A preventive GP assessment considers multiple risk factors together. What Is It? An Australian Heart Health Check is a structured cardiovascular risk assessment for eligible people without known cardiovascular disease. It may include age, family history, smoking, diabetes, blood pressure and cholesterol, and a discussion of future heart attack or stroke risk. Family history of heart disease Questions about five-year cardiovascular risk Blood pressure, diabetes or cholesterol concerns Should I Be Concerned? Talk to a GP if you are approaching the age for preventive checks, have a strong family history or are worried about diabetes, cholesterol or blood pressure. Heart Health Check Medicare eligibility depends on current criteria and your health history. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Chest discomfort that persists or spreads to an arm, jaw or back, sudden breathlessness, collapse or stroke signs require a call to 000. A preventive assessment is not intended for evaluating possible acute heart attacks. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can assess cardiovascular risk and discuss a realistic prevention plan: eating patterns, activity, smoking cessation, medicine where appropriate and scheduled follow-up. Not every patient requires every test. Bring home blood-pressure readings, recent test results and an up-to-date list of prescribed and over-the-counter medicines. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is a Heart Health Check only a blood test? No. It brings together several risk factors and a discussion of prevention goals. Does Medicare cover heart health checks? There are Medicare items for eligible patients, but eligibility and any fees must be checked for your appointment. title: Cholesterol Explained
description: Cholesterol results can be confusing because the report contains several numbers.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Blood Pressure & Heart Health Cholesterol Explained Cholesterol results can be confusing because the report contains several numbers. They become more meaningful when viewed alongside your overall cardiovascular risk. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Cholesterol results can be confusing because the report contains several numbers. They become more meaningful when viewed alongside your overall cardiovascular risk. What Is It? Cholesterol is a fat-like substance used by the body. Blood tests commonly report LDL, HDL and triglycerides. Elevated LDL can contribute to artery disease, but decisions about treatment also depend on age, smoking, blood pressure, diabetes and medical history. High LDL or triglyceride results Family history of early heart disease Questions about statin medicines Should I Be Concerned? Arrange GP review after an abnormal result, if you have a strong family history of early heart disease, or if you are unsure about a prescribed cholesterol medicine. High cholesterol itself usually has no symptoms. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Do not wait for cholesterol testing if you have persistent chest pain or symptoms of a stroke; call 000. Urgent symptoms are assessed immediately regardless of the last blood-test result. Urgent symptoms: If this is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A GP can explain your lipid results, estimate cardiovascular risk, review eating and activity patterns and discuss whether medicine would offer meaningful benefit. Repeat testing is planned according to the chosen treatment. Bring home blood-pressure readings, recent test results and an up-to-date list of prescribed and over-the-counter medicines. If unsure which appointment to choose, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Frequently Asked Questions Is all cholesterol bad? No. Cholesterol is necessary for normal body function. Different blood lipids have different roles in assessing health risk. Will diet changes always be enough? Lifestyle changes are important, but some people benefit from medicine depending on their overall cardiovascular risk. title: Understanding Cardiovascular Risk
description: What does five-year heart attack or stroke risk mean? Learn how Australian GPs assess cardiovascular risk and when to arrange a review.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles understanding your cardiovascular risk
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre | Blood Pressure & Heart Health Understanding Your Cardiovascular Risk Your cardiovascular risk is about more than one blood pressure or cholesterol reading. A GP can bring several health factors together to help you understand your future risk. Patient education Australian primary-care context Introduction Your cardiovascular risk is about more than one blood pressure or cholesterol reading. A GP can bring several health factors together to help you understand your future risk. This guide is general information for patients in Woolloongabba and neighbouring inner-south Brisbane communities. It does not replace an individual clinical assessment. What Is It? Cardiovascular disease affects the heart and blood vessels, including conditions that may lead to a heart attack or stroke. A cardiovascular risk assessment estimates the likelihood of such an event over a defined period, usually five years in the Australian primary-care setting. A GP may use the Australian cardiovascular disease risk calculator (Aus CVD Risk Calculator) for people who meet its criteria. The calculation combines factors including age, smoking, diabetes, blood pressure and blood cholesterol. It is an estimate, not a prediction of what will happen to a particular person. Should I Be Concerned? Heart and blood-vessel disease can develop before symptoms appear. A family history of early heart disease, diabetes, smoking, high blood pressure or high cholesterol is a reason to ask whether a preventive check is appropriate. If you already have cardiovascular disease, your GP will manage your established condition rather than treat a calculator result as your complete care plan. Some people need assessment outside the usual age ranges because of particular conditions or risk factors. Common Symptoms and Situations Cardiovascular risk itself usually does not cause symptoms. This is why a routine review can be worthwhile even when you feel well. Arrange a medical assessment for new breathlessness with activity, reduced exercise tolerance, palpitations or recurring chest discomfort. These symptoms need individual evaluation and should not be dismissed because a previous risk score was low. Risk factors that may be identified during a health review include elevated blood pressure, changes in cholesterol, diabetes, tobacco exposure and some family-history patterns. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Call Triple Zero (000) for suspected heart attack symptoms such as persistent chest pressure or pain, pain spreading to an arm or jaw, severe breathlessness, collapse, or stroke warning signs including facial droop, arm weakness or speech problems. Do not wait for a routine booking. For a non-emergency preventive discussion, book a GP appointment if you are in an age or risk group that may benefit from assessment, have several risk factors, or do not understand previous test results. Urgent symptoms: If someone is in immediate danger or has life-threatening symptoms, call 000. Do not use online booking for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can explain why one factor may matter more in your circumstances and, where appropriate, use the Aus CVD Risk Calculator. Together you can discuss achievable changes to smoking, physical activity, food choices, sleep, blood pressure and cholesterol. Some patients benefit from medicines, tests or additional support; others may focus first on monitoring and lifestyle changes. Your plan should account for health history, preferences, side effects, costs and follow-up needs. What Happens at the Appointment? Expect questions about family history, medicines, smoking or vaping, movement, health conditions and any symptoms. Your GP may measure blood pressure and review recent cholesterol or blood glucose results, ordering tests only when useful. If the calculator applies, your GP can discuss a five-year percentage in plain language, explain uncertainty and agree on practical next steps. Bring home blood pressure readings, prior results and your medicine list if available. Eligibility for specific Medicare-funded checks should be confirmed with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Is cardiovascular risk the same as my cholesterol level? No. Cholesterol is one risk factor. Cardiovascular risk combines several factors to estimate the chance of a heart attack or stroke over time. Does a low score mean I cannot have a heart attack? No. A low estimate means lower predicted risk, not zero risk. New or concerning symptoms always need assessment regardless of a previous score. Do I need an ECG as part of every risk check? Not necessarily. A preventive cardiovascular risk review is not the same as testing for acute heart symptoms. Your GP can explain which investigations are appropriate. Can I lower my cardiovascular risk? Many risk factors can be improved through smoking cessation, blood pressure or cholesterol treatment, movement and other changes. The best steps depend on your medical history. Trusted Australian Resources These Australian resources provide independent general health information.
